title: Deep Learning-Based Credit Risk Modeling: Addressing Data Imbalance and Invariance
venue: Journal of Trends in Financial and Economics
tldr: Integrates GAN-based data augmentation, adversarial learning, and cost-sensitive classification into a DL framework to improve credit risk prediction fairness and accuracy under class imbalance.
problem_and_motivation: Traditional credit risk models struggle with class imbalance and demographic invariance, leading to biased predictions. Existing DL methods address imbalance but fail to ensure fairness and stability across borrower segments.
approach: Uses real-world credit datasets with preprocessing via imputation, outlier detection, and autoencoder-based dimensionality reduction.
Employs GANs to generate synthetic borrower profiles for minority class augmentation, combined with SMOTE and cost-sensitive learning.
Integrates adversarial training with a fairness adversary that penalizes demographic prediction to enforce invariance across borrower groups.
Trains a hybrid feedforward-LSTM architecture using Adam optimizer with Bayesian hyperparameter tuning and ensemble learning.
Evaluates with precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC, disparate impact ratios, and equality of opportunity metrics.
findings: num: Recall for defaulters improved by 22% using GAN-based augmentation and cost-sensitive learning.
num: Overall AUC-ROC was consistently higher across multiple credit datasets compared to traditional ML models.
Adversarial training significantly reduced demographic bias in credit risk assessments.
The framework maintained stable inference speed on datasets with millions of borrower records.
Autoencoder-based feature extraction reduced dimensionality while preserving predictive features.
key_figures_tables: Figure 1: Credit Risk Prediction Accuracy Comparison → DL framework outperforms LR, DTs, gradient boosting.
Figure 2: Impact of Data Augmentation on Class Imbalance → GANs improve minority recall over SMOTE.
Figure 3: Fairness in Credit Risk Scoring (Hexbin Plot) → Adversarial training reduces demographic bias.
Figure 4: Computational Efficiency and Scalability → Stable latency across 100K-10M transactions.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper proposes a unified DL-based credit risk modeling framework combining GANs for data augmentation, adversarial learning for fairness, and cost-sensitive learning for imbalance. It demonstrates that integrating these techniques yields measurable improvements in recall for high-risk borrowers while reducing demographic bias. The framework addresses both statistical accuracy and regulatory fairness in credit scoring, contributing an approach to ethical AI in financial risk assessment.
directly_justifies: GAN-based augmentation improves recall for defaulters by 22%.
Adversarial training reduces demographic bias in credit scoring.
DL framework outperforms LR, DTs, and gradient boosting on AUC-ROC.
limits: Paper does not specify exact dataset size or source for experiments.
No statistical significance tests reported for fairness metrics.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: Systematic scan across all 14 topic domains (codes 1.A-14.C) was conducted. Topics 6.A (Predictive Modeling) and 4.B (Limitations/Gaps) were flagged as high relevance due to the paper's core contribution in DL-based credit risk prediction and its explicit identification of class imbalance and invariance gaps. Topic 6.B (Forecasting Algorithms) was rated medium as the paper uses LSTM for sequential modeling but does not focus on consumer spending forecasting. Topic 8.A (Anomaly Detection) was rated low as anomaly detection is only a preprocessing step. Topics 4.A (Landscape of Existing Systems) was contextual as background. Rejected topics: all 1.x and 2.x (Philippine-specific demographics and practices) as paper uses non-Philippine data from Chinese institutions; topics 3.x, 5.x, 7.x, 9.x-14.x are not addressed by this algorithmic credit scoring paper.

limitations: Computational cost of training GANs and adversarial networks on large financial datasets is high.
Explainability of DL-based credit assessments remains limited for regulatory compliance.
Paper lacks empirical comparison on a standardized benchmark dataset.
No ablation study isolating individual component contributions. [unacknowledged]
